title: Trust

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was emet, and your line was the seal is truth. Did one avoided truth get said, gently? Today, a trait that loosens the grip of worry. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

Hillel the elder is walking home from a journey. As he comes near the city, he hears a cry, someone screaming somewhere behind the walls. A mind can run straight home at a moment like that. Is it my street? My door? My family? The Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, tells what Hillel said instead. He said he was confident the cry was not coming from his house. He wasn't predicting the news. He had no way to know. Something in him was settled before he knew anything at all. Today's word is the name the tradition gives that settledness.
screen: `A CRY BEHIND THE WALLS.` → `NOT FROM MY HOUSE.` → `SETTLED BEFORE THE NEWS.`

segments.voice: Bitachon. Trust in God. Turn it four ways. First, the verse. The Talmud reads Hillel's calm through a line of the Psalms: the person who trusts in the LORD is not afraid of evil tidings, because the heart is steady. The trust comes first. The steadiness follows it. Second, what trust is not. Bitachon is not a guarantee that nothing hard will happen. Jewish thinkers describe it in more than one way. Some teach it as confidence that God will bring good. Others teach it as confidence that whatever comes, a person is held, even when the news is bad. Both readings live in the tradition, and both loosen worry's grip without pretending the world is safe. Third, the manna. In the wilderness, Exodus tells, bread came down each morning, and the people were told to gather only the day's portion. Those who saved some for the next day found it spoiled. Some teachers draw bitachon from that scene: enough for today, and tomorrow's portion tomorrow. Fourth, the hands still work. Bahya ibn Paquda, in his book Duties of the Heart, gives a whole section to trust, and he does not tell anyone to stop working. He describes a person who does their part with their hands and lets go of the outcome in their heart. The Psalms put the letting go plainly: Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and He will sustain thee. And trust keeps yesterday's truth company: you can look straight at a hard fact and still not be owned by it.
screen: `NOT AFRAID OF EVIL TIDINGS.` · `NOT A GUARANTEE.` · `TODAY'S PORTION TODAY.` · `HANDS WORK, HEART LETS GO.` · then, large: `CAST THY BURDEN UPON THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one worry. Settle, and breathe. Let one worry come forward, just one. Name it plainly. Then split it in two. Ask what part of it is in your hands today: a call, a form, a conversation. Hold that part, and promise it a time. Now look at the rest, the part no amount of thinking will move tonight. If you pray, you can set that part down with the words of the psalm: cast thy burden upon the LORD. If you don't, picture setting it on a table, still in sight, out of your hands. The bell holds the time.
Bitachon. Trust in God: doing your part with your hands and letting the outcome go from your heart. Today's word.
Your line: trust. Today, when the worry comes back, do the part that's yours, then say to yourself: today's portion today. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Some Jews study the Gate of Trust in Bahya ibn Paquda's Duties of the Heart, and some recite the manna passage from Exodus as part of their daily prayers as a reminder of trust.

say you're confident it isn't from your house.

fork.reveal: the Talmud says Hillel was confident the cry was not from his house, and reads his calm through the psalm about not fearing evil tidings.

original.note: Hebrew: trust, reliance, especially trust in God.

trapdoor: what you thought: trust means believing everything will be fine.
what it means: a settled heart that does its part and lets go of the outcome, even before the news comes.
what a scholar hears: Berakhot 60a, Hillel and the cry in the city, read through Psalm 112; and the Gate of Trust in Bahya's Duties of the Heart.
